title: Why are climate treaties so hard to enforce?
subtitle: From Kyoto to Paris
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Kyoto imposed binding targets, Paris bet on voluntary pledges: in both cases, major emitters walked away. Why can't states that recognize the danger keep their commitments?
author: mark-n-hoffman

hero.hook: States sign, applaud, then withdraw: no court can force a country to keep its climate promise.

blocks.text: In the summer of **2022**, extreme heat killed some **38,000 people** in Europe. Unless emissions of [[greenhouse gases]] fall, the continent could see more than **120,000 deaths** a year by 2050. In less than twenty-five years, rising seas could flood coastlines around the world every year and displace hundreds of millions of people, on top of failed harvests and illnesses linked to wildfire smoke and polluted water.

One might expect deaths by the thousands, lost homes and shortages of food and water to push governments to cooperate. Yet some of the world's biggest emitters refuse to sign global climate deals. Others withdraw from them, or fall far short of the emissions cuts needed to slow global warming.

Some governments did attempt a collective response. In **1997**, the [[Kyoto Protocol]] set legally binding reduction targets for the countries that had contributed most to global warming. Developing countries had no binding targets. The United States refused to ratify the text, arguing that those countries would not bear enough of the cost. Canada ratified it in **2002**, then withdrew ten years later.

blocks.caption: Cutting emissions costs the most polluting industries first, while their foreign competitors face no constraint.

blocks.text: Kyoto did have penalties. A country that exceeded its emissions allowance in the first period had the excess deducted from its next allowance, had to submit a compliance plan and could be barred from selling emission allowances to other countries.

Cutting emissions imposes constraints and costs on a country's most polluting industries that their foreign competitors do not face, while the benefits also flow to countries that did nothing. Every government therefore has reason to wait for others to act, even as delay makes the consequences worse. This is a [[collective-action problem]]. Negotiators need commitments that truly change behavior, but the more they demand, the less willing states are to take part.

In **2015**, the [[Paris Agreement]] took another route to attract participants: each country sets its own reduction goals. It must submit a new pledge every **five years**, act at home to meet it and report on its progress. These pledges are legally binding, but the agreement's compliance committee has no power to penalize a country that misses its targets.

This monitoring by self-reporting was meant to build trust and encourage everyone to keep their word. But it came with no enforcement mechanism, and any country could withdraw at any time. The United States left the agreement entirely in **2026**. The flexibility of Paris did attract more governments; it did not guarantee that they would honor their commitments over time.

In **1987**, the [[Montreal Protocol]] required states to ban a series of chemicals that destroy the ozone layer. Some countries received financial help to convert their factories to substitute products. This time, the commitment was actually kept, and the treaty worked.

blocks.caption: The signing ceremony of the Montreal Protocol, in September 1987.

blocks.text: By 2023, nearly 99% of the substances banned under the Montreal Protocol had been phased out. If current policies hold, the ozone layer should return to its 1980 level around 2040 over most of the globe, and around 2066 over Antarctica.

Even when a government has set itself a binding target, applying it remains hard. Closing a coal mine, for instance, turns against it the company that has invested huge sums there and the workers who lose their jobs with no time to find new ones. To implement what was signed at climate conferences, it has to win the support of these powerful interest groups.

sections.title: Cooperating in a world of rivals

blocks.text: Climate treaties are negotiated by sovereign governments, each expected to defend its national interests on the world market. They can therefore recognize a shared problem while refusing measures that threaten a powerful industry, jobs or an influential group. Agreements make cooperation possible; they also expose inaction.

blocks.caption: The Garzweiler open-pit lignite mine in the Rhineland, Germany.

blocks.text: Enforcing these agreements more strictly would require states to accept limits on their [[sovereignty]], that is, on their power to decide alone. The challenge therefore goes beyond improving the texts: the incentives to delay must change, and so must the conditions under which a government can abandon a joint commitment. In a hyper-competitive international system of nation-states, that is difficult. One thing is clear, though: without lasting cooperation, environmental catastrophe waits at the end of the road.

From Kyoto to Paris, climate agreements fail less for lack of texts than because sovereign states, in competition with one another, each have an interest in waiting for the others to pay the price of the effort.
